title: They Took Satluj Off the Internet. Now Gurudwaras Are Screening It Across Five States.
excerpt: Diljit Dosanjh's film about murdered human rights activist Jaswant Singh Khalra lasted 48 hours on ZEE5 before it was pulled. The Sikh community's response has been to open its doors wider.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Diljit Dosanjh's film 'Satluj' was removed from ZEE5 after just 48 hours.
  • Gurudwaras in five states are organizing community screenings of the film.
  • The film's release faced significant censorship challenges over four years.
  • Diljit expressed joy at community screenings, emphasizing the film's importance.
  • The film's removal has sparked discussions on historical narratives and censorship.
https://youtube.com/watch?v=zjHDjTyoWZ4

The film was online for two days. Just two days.

On July 3, Diljit Dosanjh's long-delayed Satluj — a biographical drama about Punjabi human rights activist Jaswant Singh Khalra, who exposed alleged illegal killings and secret cremations in 1990s Punjab before being abducted and murdered himself — finally premiered on ZEE5. By the evening of July 5, the platform announced the film would no longer be available for streaming in India, citing "current developments." Reports indicated the Centre directed ZEE5 to remove it under the Information Technology Rules, citing security concerns and fears the film could fuel pro-Khalistan sentiment.

The filmmakers had anticipated exactly this. Diljit later revealed they had deliberately kept the marketing campaign low-key, fearing a bigger push could have torpedoed the release entirely.

> "The community doesn't want this story to disappear simply because the film is unavailable online. If people cannot watch it on OTT, gurudwaras are opening their doors." — SGPC source to Mid-Day

But what happened next is the kind of thing streaming platforms don't have a playbook for.

A Community Mobilizes

Gurudwara committees across North India, backed by the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee (SGPC), have organized community screenings of Satluj in five states: Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, Delhi, and Jammu. The initiative is already rolling. In Jammu, four gurudwaras will screen the film between July 10 and July 13. In Jaipur, a public screening has been announced for July 11 at the Baba Fateh Singh Auditorium inside Chandi Ki Taksal Gurudwara.

> ""We will soon convene a meeting with the chairpersons of our schools and colleges," Kalka said in a statement."

In Delhi, the Delhi Sikh Gurdwara Management Committee (DSGMC) has gone further. Its president, Harmeet Singh Kalka, announced that all gurudwara committee members have been asked to download the film and begin screenings in their communities. He also called for seminars on Khalra's legacy in DSGMC-affiliated schools and colleges.

"We will soon convene a meeting with the chairpersons of our schools and colleges," Kalka said in a statement. "Seminars on Jaswant Singh Khalra will be organised in every college to discuss his life and legacy. We want people to realise the impact a single social activist can have on society."

The irony is difficult to miss. A film about a man who was silenced — kidnapped, tortured, killed — for exposing the truth is itself being suppressed. And the response from the community is to make it louder.

A Film Four Years in the Making

![Jaswant Singh Khalra — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/60/JaswantSinghKhalra.jpg)

Satluj's road to release was always going to be bruising. Completed nearly four years ago under director Honey Trehan, the film was originally titled *Ghallughara*, then renamed *Punjab '95* after the Central Board of Film Certification (CBFC) reportedly cleared it with 21 cuts. When the filmmakers challenged the decision, the CBFC's revising committee came back with 127 recommended cuts — including changes to the film's title and to Khalra's name itself.

The makers refused. The film sat in limbo for years. It eventually landed on ZEE5 as *Satluj*, uncut, under its third name — a quiet nod to the river that runs through Punjab's bloodiest history.

And then it was gone in 48 hours.

Community Screenings Surge
›Gurudwaras in five states are screening 'Satluj'.
›States involved: Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, Delhi, Jammu.
›Jammu screenings scheduled from July 10 to July 13.
›Public screening in Jaipur on July 11 at Baba Fateh Singh Auditorium.

Diljit's Response

Diljit, who has become one of the most visible Indian diaspora figures in the world — fresh off performing at the FIFA World Cup opening ceremony — took to Instagram with a still from the film and a caption that cut deep: *"The same thing that happened to Satluj also happened to Shaheed Jaswant Singh Khalra."*

In a live session with fans, the actor acknowledged he had expected the removal. "I thought the film might get banned when offices will open on Monday," he said. "But I didn't know it would happen as early as Sunday evening."

He also expressed something that sounded less like resignation and more like quiet triumph: joy at seeing gurudwaras projecting the film for their communities. "It brought me immense joy," he said. And then the line that stung the censors most: "Once something is on the internet, I don't think it can ever truly be deleted."

What This Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs — particularly Punjabi communities in the US, UK, and Canada — Satluj's removal and the gurudwara screening campaign have become about more than one film. It's become a referendum on which stories India is willing to let its own people tell, and who gets to decide when a historical truth becomes a security threat.

Censorship Journey of 'Satluj'
2019
Film completed under director Honey Trehan.
2020
Originally titled 'Ghallughara', faced 21 cuts from CBFC.
2021
CBFC recommended 127 cuts; filmmakers refused.
July 3, 2023
'Satluj' premiered on ZEE5.
July 5, 2023
Film removed from ZEE5 after 48 hours.

The film, which also stars Arjun Rampal, Suvinder Vicky, and Geetika Vidya Ohlyan, remains available on ZEE5 in international markets. For those in India, the gurudwaras are the only screen left.

Sometimes, a place of worship becomes a cinema. Sometimes, that's the whole point.
